The house resumed from Wednesday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. McKenzie (Assiniboia):
Whereas the policy of extending federal assistance to -western farmers on a bushel basis rather than on an acreage basis has worked out most unfairly and unjustly to the residents of those districts suffering from failure or near failure of crop,
And whereas a largely signed petition and memorandum has been presented to the government by the secretary of Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, praying for additional legislation to partially remedy the situation that exists,
Therefore be it resolved: that, in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to a more equitable and less discriminatory solution of this problem.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the
house on the resolution presented by the member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) I should like at the outset to make a few com-IMr. Euler.)
ments on what was brought out in the debate yesterday. For once I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) on his interpretation of the legislation in question. It seems to me that there is a misunderstanding throughout the country as to its intent. The purpose of the legislation was to grant a bonus to the farmer on each bushel of wheat that he had grown. So the man who had no wheat certainly could not participate in this bonus. I was rather amazed by the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks). Yesterday he said:
I am stating my own views to the house. The motion refers to the presentation by the representatives of the municipalities of a resolution asking for a dollar an acre. I take it that this applies to the whole province of Saskatchewan;
Now, that is not the intention of the memorandum presented to the government. I hold in my hand a copy of that memorandum, and it states very definitely what the associated rural municipalities were seeking. With the indulgence of the house I should like to read the five requests:
1.	That the Dominion government provide for a bonus in the drought areas on the seeded acreage-
Mark you, "in the drought arehs."
-for the year 1931, the basis for payment to be one dollar per acre where the crop was a total failure, and where a partial crop has been harvested and the bonus of five cents per bushel has not resulted in the farmer receiving a bonus equal to one dollar per acre, that an additional bonus be paid so that a minimum of one dollar per acre may be established regardless of the yield per acre.
I hope my hon. friend from Rosetown will observe that statement.

speechtext:
I hold in my hand a
copy of the memorandum presented to the government. The Prime Minister was kind enough yesterday to telephone the department and have this copy sent to me. Therefore, I must assume that it is an accurate copy of the presentation of the rural municipalities. Number 2 is this:
2.	That the payment of this bonus be made at the earliest possible date in order that it may be utilized for the purpose of purchasing seed and feed for 1931 spring seeding purposes and for taking care of the human necessities for the winter months, thereby relieving the Saskatchewan Relief Commission of the necessity of advancing relief to those who from the one dollar per acre bonus would be enabled to take care of their own requirements.

Farm Relief-Mr. Vallance
3.	That such payment be made only to the grower, and be subject to the same restrictions as to exemption from garnishee, assignment, etc. as is provided for under the regulations governing payment of the bonus under an act respecting wheat.
4.	That the information necessary to enable the government to make such payment be secured through the offices of the various rural municipalities in the affected area.
5.	That the parliament of the Dominion of Canada, at the next session, give careful consideration to the urgent necessity for an extension of the bonus system for the year 1932 and to the advisability of having the bonus paid on the acreage basis instead of on the bushel basis.
I will be quite frank, Mr. Speaker, in saying that this memorandum was the basis of this resolution, and it was because of the advances made iby the rural municipalities, and because of the lack of interest, or at least the dearth of information given by the government to the public that we deemed it necessary to bring in the present motion.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) suggested that only land in fit shape for putting in a crop should ibe considered, and he thought that would be one of the difficulties in administering a plan of this kind. That has been taken care of in the memorandum, which states:
In connection with suggestion No. 4 we would suggest that each grower might submit to the secretary of the municipality in which he resides a sworn statement of his seeded acreage for the year, this statement to be reviewed by the council of the municipality and the relief officer of the Saskatchewan relief commission in their district, and that a certificate of their approval be endorsed on the application before payment is recommended.
So the objection raised by the hon. member for Peace River is met in that memorandum.
As a member coming from the northern part of Saskatchewan I wish to tell the government that as far as the northern parts of the provinces are concerned, they were indebted to the government and were grateful for what was done in this regard, but I believe, and it is also stated in the memorandum, that had the government adopted the suggestion of the rural municipalities it would not have cost a great deal more than the five cent per bushel bonus cost. It was pointed out very definitely yesterday, and it has not been denied, that the bonus was a straight gift to the farmer who had wheat. We are all agreed on that. It is true also that through the interpretation placed on the word "grower" by the grain commission, many of us felt that an injustice was done. When I make that statement I have in mind individuals in all three prairie provinces, and in fact I think probably in
every province of Canada, Who are operating their farms on a one-third crop lease. Under the interpretation placed on the word "grower" by the grain commission the owner of the land received no part of the bonus. I might cite my own case as an instance. I operate a farm; I own and control everything on that farm. I pay the taxes; I pay for all repairs;
I own the equipment; I own the land, and all that the other fellow supplies is the labour. He did not receive five cents per bushel; he received 15 -cents per bushel, though I got two-ithirds of the crop -for my share because of the investment I had in the farm. I am not kicking, but that is what happened, and that injustice, or apparent injustice, was brought about in many cases by that legislation.
Now I wish to turn to the farmer in the southern part of the province, from whom this petition comes. I would urge on the government with all the force at -my command the absolute necessity, if we are to save that huge country from going down and out, of either adopting this policy or suggesting something' that will be better for that part of the country. I have pointed out that the bonus was a straight gift to the farmer in the north. The individual in the south, who was not so favourably situated, had to fill out this paper before he could get any relief, and as the hon. member for Weytburn (Mr. Young) pointed out yesterday, after the farmer gave all this information -and sold his birthright, as it were, he had to sign a note by means of which at some future date the government might -collect this money.
Yesterday the suggestion was made that probably these men never would be asked to pay these notes. Probably it would not have been a good thing to broadcast that information, because undoubtedly the western farmer is like the average individual; probably he would have asked for more relief than otherwise might have been the case if he had to sign a note, but if it is the intention of the government not to press for the collection of these notes, I think now, when the financial year is about ended and we will have either to renew this policy or bring in a new one, the time is appropriate for the government to announce to those individuals affected that these notes will not be collected.
I might deal extensively with this memorandum, but I do not think it would do much good. Some days ago I asked for copies of all correspondence that had passed-between the government and this organization, but so far I have not received those details. I should have liked them before making these remarks, because I would have been
Farm, Relief-Mr. Vallance

glad to find there some reason for complimenting the government on the action they had taken or had promised to take with regard to this memorandum, but at the moment I am not in a position to say what has been done.
I would ask the indulgence of this house to have this memorandum placed on Hansard, so that each member may read and study it. Then when the government bring down whatever relief bill is to be brought down, we will be in a better position to discuss the question from the point of view of those most vitally interested.
The memorandum is as follows:
Re: Dollar Per Acre Bonus Hon. R. B. Bennett. Premier of Canada, and Hon. Members of the Government of Canada:
The request we are making to the federal cabinet to-day is not alone for the farmers of Saskatchewan or for the people of that province, but is, we believe, for the Dominion of Canada as a whole and for the welfare of all our population. Few people appreciate that it is the great prairie sections of western Canada with their limited rainfall that has produced and will continue to produce that high protein content wheat which has made Canada famous and contributed largely to the prosperity of the whole dominion. It is also this territory that can compete with any country in the world in the growing of wheat both in low costs of production and in high quality product.
There is nothing radically wrong with western Canada or with the people who have settled in those provinces. Our present situation is the result of extreme and unusual climatic conditions for the past three years and the reduced prices which we have been compelled to accept for the produce which we have for sale and which we were forced to market at a time when the price did not meet the cost of production.
The position of the farmers in the drought area of Saskatchewan is reflected in the manner in which they have applied to municipal councils and to the relief commission for necessary relief. In 1929 only a very small percentage asked for assistance from their municipal council, and in many instances these applications were made by farmers who had suffered a severe crop loss the previous year due to hail or frost damage. In 1930, when the second crop failure occurred, the number asking for relief was greatly increased, while in 1931 we are informed that in some localities over ninety per cent of the residents have found it necessary to seek assistance. Relief to the value of over five million dollars was advanced by the rural municipalities in Saskatchewan up to the date on which the responsibility was taken over by the Saskatchewan relief commission. These advances consisted of food, fuel, clothing, fodder for live stock, gasoline and machinery repairs. The greater portion of the amounts borrowed from the banks by municipalities to enable them to grant these advances is guaranteed by the provincial government. It is a direct charge against the recipient and where he is the registered owner of the land which he operates,
(Mr Vallance.]
or where the consent of the registered owner has been secured, the amount of the relief advance is a direct charge against the land. Consequently these advances will require to be repaid at some future date. The experience of municipalities in previous years indicates that the greater proportion has been repaid.
An official of the Saskatchewan farm loan board is authority for the statement that about twenty per cent of the farmers of the province own their own land and are free from debt. He further states that another thirty-five per cent have no debts except a mortgage with the interest paid and principal reduced. Under ordinary economic conditions these people would not ask for relief from public bodies but would borrow money from loan companies, giving a first mortgage on their land as security for repayment or they would arrange for a temporary loan from the bank to tide them over the period of depression. This procedure is now almost impossible, as mortgage companies are not loaning money on this form of security and banks are consistently refusing loans to farmers, regardless of the financial position of the applicant, or the satisfactory manner in which iiis obligations to the bank have been retired in previous years. The funds of the municipalities are exhausted and the provincial government has gone as far as they can reasonably be expected to go in assisting their people. Consequently, the only assistance they can now secure is from the federal government through the agency of the relief commission. The value of relief extended in this form is expected to be repaid and the applicant signs an undertaking to that effect. No doubt the larger proportion of people will make an honest effort to pay these advances when conditions return to normal. There may be a small percentage of the residents who will secure goods from the commission and who will have little or no intention of repayment of the amount involved if that responsibility can be easily evaded. There are always a few of this class in every community, but it is not with them that we are chiefly concerned at the present time. Our interest is centred in those farmers who have been the backbone of the province, who have carried on through good years and bad, and who have made such a wonderful contribution to the building up of the great Dominion of Canada.
These people are now at the parting of the ways. Their problem is to consider whether or not further effort is worth while. Are they going to undertake the labour and expense of seeding another crop in the hope that conditions will improve and that they may regain their former position of being able to pay their debts and provide for their families the standard of living to which their labours would appear to entitle them? We submit that the morale of these people is in danger of being seriously impaired by the adversities through which they are passing, and it is the solemn duty of the government of this dominion to carefully consider the best means of assisting them at this time in order that they may retain their selfrespect and be prepared to face the future with courage and determination, in order to overcome the obstacles now confronting them.
It is for this purpose that we appear before you to-day as representatives of the farmers of Saskatchewan, and respectfully request that the assistance now being given be further extended

Farm Relief-Mr. Vallance
in the form of a direct cash payment to compensate these farmers for a small portion of their very heavy losses. There has been a heavy loss on their part as represented in their labour, wear and tear on machinery, depreciation of capital involved, and taxes where the same have been paid or allowed to accumulate, all of which have been a dead loss to the farmer.
We wish at this time to extend our appreciation to the government for the assistance which has been given to Saskatchewan through the payment of a bonus of five cents per bushel on wheat as provided for in the act respecting wheat passed at the last session of parliament. This bonus is of material assistance to those farmers in the province who are fortunate enough to have a crop to market, although we are of the opinion that a bonus on the acreage basis would have been more acceptable to a greater number of people under present conditions. We realize at the same time that certain difficulties would arise in arranging for payment on this basis, but believe these difficulties were not insurmountable and that they could have been overcome. As an example of how the present bonus applies to producers of wheat in Saskatchewan we might cite an imaginary case of two brothers, one living in the Melfort district in the north, and one living in the district surrounding Avonlea in the south. We will assume that the brother living at Melfort had two hundred acres in crop on which he had an average yield of thirty bushels to the acre. He receives from the federal treasury by way of bonus the sum of three hundred dollars, in addition to having for sale approximately six thousand bushels of wheat. The other brother has cropped a similar acreage but has had no return by reason of a crop failure and is entitled to no bonus under the regulations as they exist at the present time. This is inequitable if the purpose of the said legislation is to foster and encourage the agricultural portion of our population to continue farming their land. If it is a question of assisting only one of these two parties we submit that the one party under the present arrangement has been assisted and the brother most entitled to encouragement and assistance receives nothing.
We are not losing sight of the fact that the payments now being made are a bonus on wheat production. In might be submitted that under ordinary circumstances and with the return of normal economic conditions both in Canada and in the world at large, no bonus is necessary to encourage the farming industry, that the necessity for such a bonus only arises in times of economic disturbance such as those through which we are passing and that the bonus was proposed to encourage and assist those whose whole earnings were invested in this particular undertaking. Such being the purpose of the act, we submit that it is not functioning towards that end-that farmers who should be encouraged and assisted at the present time, and those who during the past two or three years have, owing to conditions over which they had no control, operated at a loss, in many cases a very serious one. The remedy which we claim to have discovered is to be found in the proposition which we lay before the cabinet to-day.
The 1931 seeded wheat acreage of Saskatchewan is placed at 13,881,000 acres. Statistics of the provincial department of
agriculture indicate that the average wheat yield for the past ten years' period in the province is 16J bushels per acre. Under normal conditions we would have a probable wheat crop of 222,076,500 bushels and after deducting 21 million bushels to take care of our 1932 seed requirements, we would have an aggregate of approximately 200 million bushels for sale, and Saskatchewan farmers would have received from the five cent bonus an amount approximating $10,400,000. No doubt when the bonus question was first considered by the government, the finance department were aware that such an amount would be required for the purpose mentioned. As a result of climatic conditions we find that our yield has been greatly reduced and our present estimated wheat yield for 1931 is set at 101,000,000 bushels, so that after deducting seed requirements we have 80 million bushels for market, and four million dollars will be the amount paid under the five cent bonus. Or, in other words, the amount payable under the scheme will be $6,400,000 less than it would have been had crop conditions been normal.
It was the intention of parliament that it was in the national interest of Canada that assistance in the form of a cash bonus to western farmers should be granted, and it was stated in the debate on the bill that such assistance would have an admirable effect on the morale of the people and that it would greatly lessen the amount which the government would be called upon to contribute in the form of direct relief. We submit that any money which may be paid out in the form of a cash bonus per acre will relieve to almost an equal extent the direct relief contribution of the federal government in Saskatchewan. The bonus on the bushel basis has resulted in payments to those who in many instances do not require relief in that they have a crop to market and are not under the necessity of purchasing large supplies of fodder and seed grain, while those who have had a crop failure and most urgently need assistance have not received aid except in the form of relief roadwork and direct relief through advances of fodder, fuel, food, clothing, etc. all of which is expected to be repaid. It might further be pointed out that the roadwork program carried out resulted in a number of farmers leaving their homes for the purpose of working on roads to Becure funds sufficient to take care of their families, while at the same time their farms suffered as a consequence through lack of cultivation, and additional labour would be entailed in preparing the land for seed in 1932, which will more than offset the amount which they have been able to earn from roadwork.
Believing that a measure of relief other than that at present provided for is desirable to enable the farmers in the drought area to continue in residence and operate their farms, we are requesting assistance from the federal government in the following manner.
1. That the dominion government provide for a bonus in the drought areas on the seeded acreage for the year 1931, the basis for payment to be one dollar per acre where the crop was a total failure, and where a partial crop has been harvested and the bonus of five cents per bushel has not resulted in the farmer receiving a bonus equal to one dollar per acre, that an additional bonus be paid so that a minimum of one dollar per acre may be established regardless of the yield per acre.
Farm Relief-Mr. Vallance

2.	That the payment of this bonus be made at the earliest possible date in order that it may be utilized for the purpose of purchasing seed and feed for 1931 spring seeding purposes and for taking care of the human necessities for the winter months, thereby relieving the Saskatchewan relief commission of the necessity of advancing relief to those who from the one dollar per acre bonus would be enabled to take care of their own requirements.
3.	That such payment be made only to the grower, and be subject to the same restrictions as to exemption from garnishee, assignment, etc., as is provided for under the regulations governing payment of the bonus under an act respecting wheat.
4.	That the information necessary to enable the government to make such payment be secured through the offices of the various rural municipalities in the affected area.
5.	That the parliament of the Dominion of Canada, at the next session, give careful consideration to the urgent necessity for an extension of the bonus system for the year 1932. and to the advisability of having the bonus paid on the acreage basis instead of on the bushel basis.
In connection with suggestion number four, we would suggest that each grower might submit to the secretary of the municipality in which he resides a sworn statement of his seeded acreage for the year, this statement to be reviewed by the council of the municipality and the relief officer of the Saskatchewan relief commission in their district, and that a certificate of their approval be endorsed on the application before payment is recommended. It might be pointed out that the greater portion of the municipalities in the area affected are under the operation of the Saskatchewan municipal hail insurance scheme, and the municipality has a record of the seeded acreage of all parcels of land which have not been withdrawn from the operations of the municipal hail insurance act. These acreages are authentic in that they were reported before June 10, and it is on the owner's statement of acreage in crop that the municipal hail rates are levied. Consequently it would not be to the farmer's advantage to report an acreage in excess of that actually sown. Further confirmation, if necessary, could be secured from the census returns. There would be no cost to the government in so far as the securing of information on this basis is concerned, as we have the assurance of municipal officials that they will take care of any necessary cash outlay for securing the required statistical information to enable payment to be made.
From the figures quoted it is evident that our wheat production in Saskatchewan this year is about forty-four per cent of normal, and if the same percentage applies to the acreage basis our proposal would call for payment of fifty-six per cent of 13,881,000 acres or a total outlay on the wheat acreage of $7,773,300. The total seeded acreage of other grains is as follows:

Total cOarse grain acreage. . 7,246,000 
The percentage of loss of the coarse grains crop is not so great as wheat for the reason that seeding of same was later in the season and the rainfall during the latter part of July in some districts materially assisted growth. A reasonable estimate of the crop loss in coarse grains would be forty per cent, or approximately three million acres. This amount, added to our above estimate of the amount which would be payable in respect of the seeded w'heat acreage gives a total of $10,773,360.
When our proposal was submitted to Honourable E. B. Bennett and Honourable Robert Weir at Eegina in the month of August and was later refused by the premier, we undertook to secure an expression of opinion from the farmers of the province regarding the matter. For this purpose a series of meetings were held at various strategic points throughout the province at which the proposal was placed before the people for discussion and consideration. In every instance unanimous approval was given and we were strongly urged to again take the matter up with the federal cabinet and to press for reconsideration of their previous unfavourable decision. We further have in our office and present to you to-day resolutions and petitions from various public bodies throughout the province of Saskatchewan supporting our application. Approximately two hundred rural municipal councils have by resolution given their approval and the petitions submitted herewith contain the names of upwards of five thousand farmers. In addition, many resolutions have been received from individual ratepayers' meetings of the municipalities. Eesolutions and petitions have also been received from various other organizations such as ratepayers' associations, cooperative trading associations, boards of trade, and councils of urban municipalities.
In presenting this request to the government we are confident that our application for a bonus on the acreage basis has the support of practically one hundred per cent of the people of the province of Saskatchewan, regardless of whether they are resident in the drought areas or not. Other areas of the province fortunate enough to have a crop to market this year also support our request. We therefore respectfully urge that this matter again be carefully considered by your cabinet, and assure you that a decision to grant our request would be most favourably received by the people of the province we represent.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
The
greater part of the problem facing the government in connection with agriculture to-day is chiefly due, in my opinion, to the extraordinary decline in the prices of farm commodities as compared with those of manufactured and other products. The last report of the Bank of Nova Scotia clearly pointed out this fact, and it was also made evident in the report of a year ago. An examination of the statistics in this connection will indicate that prices of farm products have declined from 35 per cent to 40 per cent, and in some cases even more, while wholesale prices have declined from 20 per cent to 25 per cent at the most, and retail prices from 11 per cent to

Farm Relief-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
15 per cent. Undoubtedly it was a recognition of this extraordinary disparity between the price level of agricultural commodities and that of the goods the farmers must buy that was an influence in inducing the administration a year ago to institute this so-called five cent bonus. The question was discussed in this house, and at that time some speakers on the government side described it as an alleviation by way of reduction in freight rates, that is, that it was supposed to pay a part of the cost of freight. Others said it was a measure of direct relief; others described it as a bonus, while many people throughout the country have looked upon it as a straight gift. It was also explained as compensation for the tariff, but no one with any sanity could ever regard a five cent bonus on wheat as a compensating adjustment for the tariff. There is no doubt in my mind on that point. It would require many times that amount per bushel, under present price levels, to recompense the farmers for the enormous costs in connection with tariff adjustments of this and previous years.
The point I want to make is that the government cannot solve the present problem of agricultural conditions by mere miserable bonuses or bounties. If applied on a sufficiently large scale to one branch of industry such a scheme might afford temporary relief, but that could be done only at the expense of the taxpayers of the whole country. This bonus in the long run falls on the backs of the taxpayers and comes ultimately out of those classes that are the least organized and the most unprotected in regard to their own price levels. We have no power over the price levels of our own commodities. It has been alleged that at one time we attempted to secure this by organization of the wheat pools, but no effort was made-and I have the word of every officer of the wheat pools- to try unnecessarily or unduly to increase the price level. The whole object of wheat pooling was to try to eliminate many of the intervening costs in the actual handling and marketing of grain and so to improve the position of the grain grower. But so long as the farmers of this country must depend on export markets for the principal bulk of their commodities, and so long as export market prices govern prices in this country, nothing in the way of bonuses is any answer to the problem facing us.
I have just received one or two letters in connection with this matter. It is true .that in certain districts that had very large or reasonably large crops there was an expression of aipipreciation of this five cents a bushel
cheque that came along. Undoubtedly it may have helped some of these men to pay their threshing bills. But the fact of the matter is that even with the bonus the price received by the farmer was far below the actual cost of production, and this gave no recognition whatever to general agricultural conditions. The result is that to-day agriculture as a whole is in a worse position than it was a year ago. I have a letter dated .January 12, from Redland, Alberta, in which the following statement is made:
I will cite the case of one farmer which will illustrate that of many others. This man threshed enough wheat for his spring seeding and has been compelled to sell this wheat in order to merely live through the winter. He said they had been going to bed at dark to save the price of kerosene. Of course there are other farmers who didn't thresh any wheat.
Now I am aware that you understand this impossible situation as well as I. You see the man who sells his wheat is not permitted to get seed from the government even though he has nothing left. Surely this situation can be righted. Comparing him with the man who raised a bumper crop and received a bonus besides should be sufficient.
Another matter freely discussed was the fact that people in this drought area are being pressed to the limit for collections by oil and machinery companies, and even the banks. The method of compounding interest by some of these collectors would make Shyloclc look like a philanthropist.
That last statement touches one crucial aspect of the problem in which undoubtedly the government could be of material assistance to us. I urge upon the administration the calling of a federal conference of all the mortgage companies, loan companies and banks in order to find out whether or not the private financial interests in Canada are willing to undertake to carry their share of this load of depression. It is utterly unfair to ask the primary producer, whether he be farmer or fisherman, to carry this gigantic load of increasing interest rates-not decreasing rates- in the face of existing conditions. I have another letter which comes from the acute drought district. And may I at this stage suggest to the government that we in Alberta feel that there has not been fair treatment of the drought area in that province as compared with the treatment meted out, poor though it may have been, to the farmers in Saskatchewan. Our province has not had any share of that 100 per cent relief granted by the federal government. An hon. gentleman suggests that we are not Tory enough. Well, I am rather proud of that; I hope we shall never be Tory enough in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. But I have this to say. In common with my hon. friend from Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and my' hon. friend from Medicine Hat
314	COMMONS
Farm Relief-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
(Mr. Gershaw), I represent a constituency which is almost entirely within the drought area. Last year and the year before there were very small crops and very low prices, and this year we were almost completely wiped out. Practically the entire area is a total failure. These men have nothing to sell for which they will receive a profit, and how they will finance this year's operations, without any cash in their pockets, is a problem which they cannot solve. Now if agriculture is to be regarded in the future as the principal industry of this country, it is vitally necessary that this government should undertake a definite scheme now, and not later, to see that these men have, by some means or other, sufficient resources to secure the necessities for seeding and harvesting operations for this year. They have no resources whatever, but that is not because they have not gone into mixed farming. To the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) let me say that I have long held the view that those who attempted to explain conditions in western Canada by saying that we had no diversified farming but were putting all our eggs in one basket were speaking exceedingly stupidly or without a sufficient consideration of the facts. The fact is that per head of population we produce more diversified products in western Canada than are produced in any other part of the dominion. But what of it? Suppose we embraced wholeheartedly the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture with regard to diversified farming.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Will the hon. member inform the house when I have ever made any statement with regard to diversified farming in western Canada, either in this house or anywhere else?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: At no time, as far as I aim aware, have I ever advocated diversified farming as the cure-all for the ills of western Canada or of any other part of the country.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that, and I sincerely trust that the newspapers will interpret his statement correctly this time. He is quite right; it is not a cure-all and will not even modify conditions at the present time. The only effect of diversified farming at the 'present time is that the farmer may be able to live a little longer under this rotten system of 
injustice than he otherwise might. That is all; he can drag out a miserable existence on the products he is raising at a loss. Under date February 11, 1932, the following letter has come to hand:
This district on the whole in 1931 did not thresh as many bushels of wheat as was sown, and the complete failure of oats, barley and rye forced a great number of farmers to drive a portion of their live stock great distances to irrigated districts and trade or exchange them, usually at a sacrifice, for feed to keep the remainder of their stock alive.
The 1931 crop failure, following as it did the light crop and poor prices of 1929 and 1930 which reduced the farmer to a point financially where he had to put forth every effort to finance seeding of the 1931 crop, places him in a position where his hardships can hardly be exaggerated.
I know they cannot be.
The prices of the farm produce at the present time are:
Eggs: 10 cents per dozen.
Butter: 8 cents per pound.
Cattle: 2 cents per pound.
Hogs: 2J cents per pound.
With the price levels as given in this letter, and which I know prevail in the district spoken of in the southern part of my constituency, it is utterly hopeless for these unfortunate farmers to expect to carry on during this year. They have not been able to obtain a sufficient revenue from the small herds of stock or flocks of poultry to keep body and soul together, much less to buy the necessary clothing for themselves and their children.
Under these circumstances, I submit that an entirely new agricultural policy involving a change in other directions is also required. So long as this government continues, as have preceding governments, to press down upon the primary producer who is carrying the load of the development of industrialism, just so long will agriculture be placed under a handicap and sooner or later it will vanish. This government through the imposition of unfair customs duties has increased unnecessarily our difficulties; it has succeeded in pegging the prices of manufactured products while we have had to take what we can get in the foreign markets. So convinced of this fact was the annual convention of the United Farmers of Alberta, that this year it passed the following resolution:
Whereas, the fiscal policy known as protection or a protective tariff which has been on trial in Canada for over fifty years since its inauguration in 1879, has belied every promise of its promoters, both then and since, and has utterly failed to promote the general well-being of the people of Canada and has developed instead a most pernicious maldistribution of our wealth, and is on this account immediately responsible for that disparity in market values as expressed in present day prices, which exists

Farm Relief-Mr. Cowan (Long Lake)
between what the farmer sells and what he buys, which disparity is one of the principal causes of the present industrial debacle and the general economic depression;
Be it therefore resolved, that the time has come for an immediate all round reduction in our custom duties to the intent that within a period of not less than five years every feature and constituent of this barbaric economic superstition be eliminated from the fiscal policy of our country.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman endorse that?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Who wrote it?

speechtext:
I am informed that it was written by a well known Presbyterian minister in the constituency of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy). In itself, it is a tribute not only to the intelligence but to the penmanship of the people of that constituency.
There are many other factors which affect agriculture, but at the present time the two principal ones are, first, the enormous load of debt and interest charges and, second, the unfair position in which agriculture is placed in relation to other producers of manufactured goods. Unless there is a modification downwards of our capital obligations plus an elimination if possible, or at least a considerable reduction in interest rates, I venture to predict that it will be difficult to bring about a recovery of agriculture in western Canada. This prediction may be pessimistic and gloomy, but it is the fact.
No new markets have been discovered to extend the sale of our products. Foreign markets are rapidly narrowing due to the stupid nationalism of certain European countries, in which stupidity we are now the supreme participator. How this country expects to continue to keep alive an industrial expansion which has been the result of available f oreign markets by a policy of restriction, by continuing a stupid fiscal policy which does not operate, is beyond my understanding. Until this administration about faces with its fiscal policy and either by international agreement or by frank action on its own part attempts to break down the barriers between nations or to open up new markets for our products, there is but little hope for the future of agriculture in Canada.
I grant that the modification of our policy in regard to banking and credit and the creation of national control and planned distribution of our whole monetary machine will have a healthy and salutary effect upon the internal consumption of manufactured goods, but unfortunately agriculture is not in the same position. We must continue to sell abroad the great bulk of our commodities.
Take wheat alone; in a normal year we can expect a crop of 450,000,000 to 500,000,000 bushels. Of that crop we sell abroad all but
150.000.	000 bushels. It might be possible to increase internal consumption by 25,000,000 or
50.000.	000 bushels, but that still leaves an enormous surplus to be shipped overseas and for which surplus we must take a price determined by international competition in the limited foreign markets available. Even a financial reform along the lines advocated by those of us in this corner of the house can have but little real effect upon market conditions. Unless this government undertakes a drastic alteration in its policy with regard to international trade at will be deliberately damning agriculture to a steady decline.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate seems to be an attempt to discover whether or not the 'farmers of western Canada are satisfied with the relief which has been granted, first, in the form of the five cent bonus on wheat grown last year, and, second, by means of the measures adapted to apply in those territories where the 'bonus was not paid. As I understand it, some $10,000,000 has been paid out to the farmers of western Canada through this bonus.
I have yet to meet or hear of a farmer who refused to accept that five cent bonus. I never knew of a system to be put into force which gave greater satisfaction than this. No one has made any money out of the administration of .this bonus; it is not a rich man's job at all. Hundreds of thousands of farmers have benefited, and I have yet to hear of a single instance where the money was misapplied, misappropriated or misdirected. The government is deserving of congratulation upon the business methods pursued in the handling of this bonus.
During the early part of last session this five cent bonus was discussed, by many Saskatchewan members and others. At that time none of us had any intimation of the calamity which was to occur because of the drought which affected many portions of the west. We were very glad to be granted this bonus and at that time it was understood that it would apply to the whole province of Saskatchewan. As far as the intentions of the government were concerned, there was no thought of discrimination. Later on a very large area covering some 200 municipalities become badly drought-stricken, and it was evident that the five cent bonus would not apply to them, because there was nothing on which that five cent bonus could be paid. What was to be done? Were we to ask the government or was the government to ask parlia-
316	COMMONS
Farm Relief-Mr. Cowan (Long Lake)
ment to abandon the whole proposition because some 200 municipalities out of probably 1,000 would be unable to secure any benefits under this plan?
The only course for the government to pursue was to carry on along the lines already adopted. In spite of criticism we decided what we were going to do and we did it. Then, when this new drought condition arose, it became the duty of the government and of parliament to devise new methods to meet that new condition. That was done. It was decided that a relief commission should be appointed to administer relief affairs in those areas. That has been carried out. The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) has presented a new proposal, namely, that this dollar per acre scheme should be handled by two different bodies, by the municipalities and the relief commission. It is impossible for one and the same thing to be handled by two different bodies.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS

member to address the chair.

The relief
commission operating in those areas is the most complete relief organization I ever saw. They have disbursed millions of dollars. We must remember the extent of the country. There were more than 200 municipalities to be covered and a new organization had to be created. There were 250,000 people, who were scattered over hundreds of miles, thrown into a state of destitution and they had to be provided for. The facts had to be ascertained; men had to be appointed and committees had to be formed in those different areas. This took time and at the beginning hon. gentlemen had their opportunity, but they were not equal to their job. While this preliminary work was being done, the people were in a state of dismay; they did not know what was ahead of them; so far as they could see, nothing was being done. But the committee set to work and created their organization. First they laid down their plans, and then, having laid down their plans, they proceeded slowly, surely and in a most conservative way to carry them out.

When my hon. friends bring this up as a substitute for the plan that we now have, I do not wonder they

Farm Relief-Mr. Beynon
are in a quandary; they have no argument. Let them keep quiet and we shall finish the job.
I have described the situation as it is and, as I say, the operations of the relief commission have been carried out successfully. I think it is well the people should know this, because the money is coming out of the public treasury. It was decided that the outlying posts should be the first places covered in order that there would be no trouble in such areas should a blizzard suddenly come up and catch them unawares. After the outlying parts were covered, they gradually crept in and covered the areas closer in according to their drought-stricken condition.
This is the result. Three weeks ago a gentleman in Regina who travels constantly throughout southern Saskatchewan, who knows conditions there and who has no personal interest in the matter, said to me: "Cowan, if a single child had died of starvation in the province of Saskatchewan, wouldn't the Grits have raised a deuce of a holler?" There has not been a single death through starvation or neglect. The administration has been excellent. Not very long ago a big farmer accosted me in a village in my constituency. He said:	"There is my farm; I have put
$30,000 into that farm and it is not worth anything now to me. I have not a dollar and I cannot get one, but the relief commission is supplying me and my family with what I require and I am taking everything from them with thankfulness." That is the spirit in which the people out there are receiving the commission. They know that the commission is doing the best they can. I would also point this out to my hon. friends across the way. I know that they can never see a day ahead. The Liberals never can and never could. They want all the money spent right now.
There is one thing more we know, Mr. Speaker. We know that these people are being carried now. We know also that if we spend millions and millions now, they will all be wasted unless something else happens. These people must be provided with the means of carrying on their operations next summer. Seed has to be provided. With my hon. friends across the way knowing all that which is yet before us, staring us in the face, and it will cost at the very least $15,000,000, would they have us spend all our money now, and if so, where are the farmers going to get their seed? All these things have to be taken into consideration, and we have to reserve a sufficient amount in our treasuries to carry our people. But a year from now
our hon. friends opposite will look back and will then admit that we, the Conservative party, have dealt with the people out there very generously and have done our work, and have done it mighty well.

That provision of the act I think was one of its wisest. The situation is simply this: In western Canada perhaps 75 per cent of the farms are mortgaged, and in a great many cases the original owner who mortgaged the land to a mortgage company is now operating the land on a lease from the mortgage company, and had it not been for the provision in the act that the actual producer of the grain shall get that five cent a bushel bonus a large part of the bonus would have gone to the mortgage companies.

I doubt very much, Mr. Speaker, if
agriculture can tax itself into prosperity. Looking at the estimates we find that one of the big increases this year is an increase in interest of $30,000,000, which looks as if we could not tax ourselves into prosperity.
On general principle I am opposed to the idea of a bonus, but speaking for Ontario farmers, if the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat will keep the western wheat farmer growing wheat I think it would be worth while to the farmer of Ontario in order to keep the western farmer out of mixed farming, which is ruining the Ontario farmer. So looking at it from that point of view, not that it makes any difference because the government does what it likes, I suppose for the time being we had better support the bonus because if any more mixed farming products come upon the markets of Ontario from the west things are going to be even worse for the farmers of Ontario. I had never believed that mixed farming was the solution of western conditions. True, it would give the western farmer more to eat, since that is all he has at the moment, but it would also give him more lines on which he could lose money. Mixed farming suits Ontario, and if the prairie provinces go into mixed farming it will be very disastrous for

Farm Relief-Mr. Mullins
this province. So, speaking for my agricultural constituency, for the present I support the bonus on wheat. I do not believe in it, but it may for the time being keep the western wheat farmer running after the five cents and not encourage him to do the thing that we do not want him to do.

speechtext:
It
had not been my intention, Mr. Speaker, to participate in this debate, but when I hear so many hon. members on the other side making a political handle of the resolution I have to take a hand in it too. I represent a purely agricultural constituency in western Canada; it has not got a single smokestack in any part of it. When I am speaking of conditions in that constituency I do so from personal experience. My life has been forged on the anvil of experience, and not in a university as was my friend's from Bow River (Mr. Garland); I never had the opportunity of even scratching my back up against a college wall; but when it comes to practical experience on the prairies, probably I have had as much as any one of my hon. friends opposite.
To substantiate what I am going to say I want to read this little clipping which I cut from the Manitoba Free Press a few days ago:
Forty Years Ago To-day
H. A. Mullins, well known live stock exporter

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

That is all right.
-had taken hold of the well known Binsearth stock farm at Binsearth, Manitoba.
That was forty years ago. For forty years I have been farming on the prairies of western Canada, and probably what I shall say will have some little weight to keep up the spirits of some of those whining Jerusalem demigods. I remember well in the old days on the prairies when produce was much cheaper than it is to-day. I remember coming to the city of Toronto with a trainload of hogs. I came under the pressure of that multimillionaire that my hon. friends opposite talk about and I sold the shipment for four cents a pound. What happened? The following year hogs were worth eight to eight and a half cents a pound. I told him that I had devoted the best part of my life to the improvement of live stock and farming generally in an endeavour to get away from exclusive grain growing, and I could not understand why ho would write an article like this. To the mortgage companies, I say, "Keep your hands off the poor man." Some farmers have been inclined to be extravagant and have speculated in the stock market, and a number of them have gambled in grain. Having had their crops destroyed, they could not take advantage of the five cent bonus granted last year. A petition signed by a large number of farmers in the hail-swept areas was sent to the Department of Agriculture requesting action similar to that mentioned in the resolution. I believe, however, the hon. member for Marquette arose in his place to deal with this matter in a humorous vein rather than in the vein that has been suggested by this resolution, which is a specific one dealing with a specific subject. Most of the hon. members who have spoken during the past hour and a half have spoken about everything but that which is contained in the resolution.
The resolution refers simply to those farmers who were hailed out or who, through some other act of God, were unable to secure any advantage out of this five cent bonus that was legislated here last year. I do not rise to discuss the principle of the bonus or to support that principle; what I do wish to speak of is the inequitable manner in which the farmers of the west have been treated with respect to this legislation. Yesterday I asked an hon. member who, I believe, is a very brilliant lawyer, the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) what he thought about the bonus. He said that the bonus is nothing but a subvention to the farmer. I asked him whether he thought the bonus was a relief measure and he said that the bonus under no circumstances was legislated in this house as a relief measure. I cannot understand the difference between a bonus and a relief measure. If an industry in this country is in bad straits and needs help, the government gives it a bonus. Why give it a bonus if that industry is not in bad straits? On the same grounds if agriculture were not in bad straits, why should we legislate to give five cents for every bushel of wheat raised on the western prairies last year? In that respect I consider this five-cent piece was a relief measure to the farmers in the west. It was a relief measure to the extent that there was a great disparity between the price the farmer was getting for his products and the price he had to pay for other goods and services. It was an aid to the farmers of the west and in my estimation it certainly was a relief measure to aid those farmers who were not receiving an adequate price for their wheat.
The hon. gentleman referred to some hon. members as university graduates, or as men who scratched their backs on the walls of a university. If scratching one's back is necessary, I do not see any difference between

Farm Relief-Mr. Porteous
scratching one's back on a university, or a church or a hall, or on the gatepost of some farm.
I have under my hand a resolution which was passed in my own district and which reads:
Whereas, all the hailed-out farmers are in the poorest financial position of any other Canadian farmer; and
Whereas, we will ultimately have to pay to the dominion treasury our share of the bonus now paid per bushel of wheat; and
Whereas, the bonus does not relieve the farmer who was hailed out and went to nearly as much expense in growing a crop; and
Whereas, this bonus had incurred an added burden on such farmers in that they have to pay five cents extra for all feed and seed; and
Whereas, the purchasing power of said farmers has been reduced to worse than nothing by reason of said disaster; therefore be it
Resolved, that the federal government make arrangements to pay a bonus of one dollar per acre on the hailed-out acreage of wheat and that such acreage be determined from the 1931 census returns.
I repeat that the question is not so much on the principle of the bonus as on the application of it. If the hailed-out farmer is not going to receive any benefit from this five-cent piece, I should like to know what alternative there is for those farmers who have been hailed out? In my district, to the south of me, there is a stretch of territory about 100 miles long and ten miles wide that has been hailed out; in the north there is another stretch of territory 100 miles long and ten miles wide that has also been hailed out. The people in those areas are receiving absolutely no benefit from the legislation parliament passed last year. I do not think this is fair to those farmers who, through no fault of their own, have no crops to take to the elevator and therefore do not receive the five-cent piece for each bushel haled there. I believe, in lieu of this five-cent piece, in lieu of this aid, the people who have been hailed out are entitled to some alternative to the legislation which was passed last year.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the previous speaker, that much of the discussion has centred, not on the bonus but on other points that have arisen in the debate on the resolution which is at present before the house. The reason why last year legislation was enacted providing a bonus of five cents on wheat was that there were several complaints as to the price of wheat. I should like to direct the attention of the house to the fact that the price of wheat has materially increased in the last year, and I believe that average increase is in the neighbourhood of fifteen cents a bushel.
I should like to point out also that during that period other agricultural products have decreased in price. Therefore if the wheat grower is to be bonused, other producers of agricultural products should also be bonused. We have heard complaints from northern Saskatchewan because they were not in relief districts; we have heard complaints from southern Saskatchewan because they did not receive a bonus, but so far as the debate has proceeded on this resolution, we have not heard complaints from the vast majority of the farmers in the rest of the dominion.
The question of relief has been spoken of in connection with this resolution. I am not in a position to comment upon that except that I believe that relief should be given in any area where there is no crop and where the farmer of necessity needs relief. As regards bonuses, I am not in favour of them, but if we are to bonus one branch of agriculture, we should bonus all branches of agriculture which are suffering just as much as the wheat grower. We should not single out the wheat grower and give him a bonus while the man who grows oats or other grain is not bonused. If the government is contemplating any further legislation in that regard the bonus should apply to all branches of agriculture and to all parts of the dominion.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I am very sorry that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) has left the chamber. I hope he will avail himself of the first opportunity to make in his own constituency the same address that he made here this afternoon. Might I add that I am sure the opportunity will be afforded him almost any time at his convenience, and if there is any hiding to be done, I think it will be my hon. friend who will do it. In his discourse this afternoon he quite conveniently left out that part of his speech he usually makes where he takes around with him his cream can. I must confess that I cannot see that his speech had anything to do with the matter that is really under discussion this afternoon, namely, the application of the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat.
I listened yesterday to the very fine distinction made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) with respect to the application of the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat and the giving of direct relief. If I understood him correctly, he placed the five cents a bushel bonus on one side, as applying to one particular need, and direct relief on the other, for another purpose. I have no objection whatever to that division. In fact, I think
326	COMMONS
Farm Relief-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
that is exactly how it has worked out. So far as the farmers of my own constituency are concerned they were mighty glad to receive the five cents a bushel bonus cheque with the signature of the Prime Minister upon it-that is, those who got it. But the problem is in taking care of the class of farmers who had some crop on which they could receive some money by way of the five cents a bushel bonus, as contrasted with the class of farmers dependent on direct relief. I could name a large number of farmers in my constituency who this year did not thresh as much grain as they sowed last spring. I could name other farmers who got less than 1,000 bushels of all kinds of grain from a half-section of land. This class of farmers could not participate in the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat simply because they had to keep all their grain for feeding purposes; nor on the other hand can they claim that they had a complete crop failure. I doubt very much if a crop that yields 1,000 bushels from a half-section is of any benefit at all. It might just as well be regarded as a complete crop failure. At the present time I know of several farmers in my constituency who are hauling two year old wheat straw for feeding purposes a distance of eight to twelve miles. I am told that along a certain highway running about twenty-five miles, thirty dead horses can be seen from the road. The local veterinary tells me that he has never before had as many calls to attend sick horses as he has this winter; and he attributes the sickness to lack of feed.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, we had an invasion of grasshoppers in our district last year. They covered quite a large area and did considerable damage. I am not sure that we really know how much damage they did to our grain. Whether or not these grasshoppers damaged our feed, such as we have, particularly roughage, to any great extent I do not know. The fact of the matter is that such feed as our district has does not seem to have substance, with the result that we are not getting results from the feeding it.
I have in mind also another district which previous to two years ago had really three successive crop failures, not from drought, not from drifting, but, as hon. members may be surprised to learn, from flooding. Here is the situation in that area. They had a fair crop last year and again this year, and on this year's crop they secured the five cents a bushel bonus, but having had two or three successive crop failures previous to that, and with the low price of grain prevailing, they are hardly in any better position than if 
they had had no crop at all this year. If these farmers had had a complete crop failure they would have been able to participate in direct relief, but as they had some crop, they must simply carry on as best they can, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they are not carrying on very well. The farmers I speak of are between the divisions which the hon. member for Regina has described. They had a little crop, so it cannot be said they had a complete crop failure, but they did not have sufficient crop on which they could sell any appreciable amount of grain from which they could get the benefit of the five cents a bushel bonus. They have no money, they cannot borrow any. The municipalities in which they live are not in a position to assist them, and are certainly unable to meet the situation. More than that, the provincial government is not in a position to materially assist them. The particular municipalities that I have in mind-and I hesitate to refer to this-a year ago only collected something over 50 per cent of their taxes, and last year only in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent. It is very easy to see therefore that they are quite unable to meet the situation.
I have been in touch with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) on this matter, and I am satisfied that he realizes the situation that prevails. I know it is a very large problem, one with far-reaching effects, but I do want the house to appreciate the disadvantage suffered by the man who is in between the one who can qualify to receive some benefit from the five cents a bushel bonus and the man who has had a complete crop failure. He is in a very difficult position, and I know of my own knowledge that in many cases he is not able to carry on and put in a crop, let alone maintain his live stock until the grass grows, unless he receives some form of assistance. It is necessary to have feed shipped in from a distance, carload lots of hay and grain, and the freight charge increases the price about 30 per cent. Surely there is some opportunity for relief in that direction.
I hope before this debate closes the Minister of Agriculture or some member of the government will be able to tell the house of some policy which the government is prepared to adopt to relieve the situation which I have described. It is essential that something be done, and if we can look forward to some definite policy to meet the situation I for one will certainly give it my wholehearted support.
There is another matter in connection with the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat to which I might refer. We in the province of

Farm Relief-Mr. Brown
Manitoba produce ordinarily about 50 per cent, roughly speaking, of the barley grown in western Canada. That is an important item with us. Barley is one of our main cash crops, yet we are not in a position to receive anything in the way of a bonus on barley when we come to ship it to other parts of Canada. We also find that the freight rate is such that we cannot ship it locally without being subjected to excessive freight costs. It is more to our advantage to ship it for export rather than for domestic use. That is the situation, and I think it is only fair to say, although I do not want to draw any distinction, this five cent per bushel bonus on wheat in reality acts more to the advantage of Saskatchewan and Alberta than it does to Manitoba.
Mr. Speaker, I think the federal assistance to our western farmers would have worked out much more equitably if it had been applied on the basis as suggested in this resolution, and for that reason I shall lend it my support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I agree with what the member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) has said, that very much of this discussion has been entirely outside of the matters referred to in the resolution itself. It is not my intention at this time to enter into a discussion of the general situation that confronts agriculture. I hope that we shall have an opportunity of doing so before the close of the session.
So far as the five cent bonus is concerned, I do not think there was any particular need for members on the other side to come to the defence of the government in regard to it. It was not opposed by any member on this side of the house, and so far as those who received the bonus were concerned, I am certain they received it gladly. So far as I know the question was not discussed by any bodies of organized farmers in Manitoba. True, at the annual convention of the United Farmers of Manitoba we did make a very clear declaration that we did not accept the five cent bonus as a "compensating adjustment," as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) referred to it a year ago, for certain other disabilities under which we labour. I tried to make that point clear in the house a year ago. We accepted the five cent bonus as an earnest of the willingness of the government to help the western farmers to bear the very serious losses that they had incurred during the last two or three years.
I do not think it was worth while making any fine distinctions-such, for instance, as the member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) made
-between the five cent bonus subvention to the growers of wheat and the relief measures that were necessitated in other parts of the province. I hope at some future time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) will develop his argument and tell us what the distinction is between mixed farming, balanced farming and diversified farming. I shall listen with a good deal of interest when he expounds his views on the matter. Foolishly I had thought those were three different terms for the same thing. However, perhaps my mind is not capable of grasping those very fine distinctions.
I am sorry that the member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) is not in the chamber, for I received a message from a friend of mine the other day that I should like to deliver to him in the hearing of the house.
I think we should turn our thoughts definitely to the resolution before the house. It seems to me that if we keep our minds fixed upon it we need not carry on the discussion at very great length. Undoubtedly the particular measures of relief that the government adopted last session have not worked out equitably. I do not think it needs any argument to prove that. There are farmers in the northern part of the prairie provinces who reaped large harvests, and they got their five cents per bushel bonus. It is not at all to the point for the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) to say that even that bonus did not put farming on a profitable basis. To carry out his argument logically, it would be better if the farmers had small crops instead of large. The district I represent is in the same condition as the district represented by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir). It is an open question whether a crop that barely pays the cost of harvesting places the farmer in any better position than if he had a complete crop failure. I have seen crops hailed out, and the farmer in grave doubt as to whether it would pay the cost of harvesting. Everybody who has farmed and who has had experience of hail damage knows that. In very many cases when the farmer has harvested his hailed crop he has found he would have been very much better off had he not touched it at all. This is true of the situation that prevails in many sections of Manitoba-not a complete crop failure, but so close to it that the crop itself did not pay the cost of harvesting.
The situation that confronts us, as the member for Macdonald has pointed out, is that a very large number of farmers find themselves short of feed, their horses and cattle are dying,
32S
Farm Reliej-Mr. Brown

and up to the present, wherever the fault lies, they have not been able to get any measure of relief. As a result in the coming spring many of those farmers will be unable to provide themselves with the necessary feed and seed in order to put in their crops. I visited the centre of my constituency a short time ago, and there met forty or fifty farmers at an afternoon meeting. They laid their case before me very fully. It is a comparatively small district, but they told me that they would need in the neighbourhood of twenty-five hundred bushels of wheat, oats and barley for seed, and about six thousand bushels of oats in order to feed their horses while they were putting in their crop. As has been pointed out, the municipalities are not in a position to give that assistance. Before I left for Ottawa I made it a point to get in contact with the secretaries of the municipalities, and I would judge that even the best of them had not up to the first of January been able to collect more than forty per cent of their taxes. One municipal secretary wrote to me that they had $75,000 of unpaid taxes on their books, and owed the schools $50,000. So it is no use looking to the municipalities to provide relief. Neither is it any use to look to the provincial governments, for they are now at their wit's end so far as finances are concerned. I fully realize that even the Dominion government could not borrow enough money to recoup the farmers for the losses they have sustained during the last two or three years. Still the Dominion government, more than any other governing body, is in a position to afford some measure of relief, and this is a situation we must face. It is true that it will be a measure of relief to the individual farmer, but it is also a great national question which this parliament should consider. As far as possible we should give such help as will ensure that the land which properly should be seeded in grain will be so seeded. At the moment it may seem that the raising of wheat is being carried on at a loss, nevertheless it is true and will continue to be true in the future that the wheat crop is the one thing above all others on which we must depend for the prosperity not only of the western farmer but of all lines of industry east and west, since the sale of the wheat crop in late years has been our one source of new wealth.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think I shall content myself at the moment with emphasizing these paints and lending my support to the resolution which has been presented to the house, the effeot of which I think is perfectly well understood. The giving of the five cent bonus

has not worked out equitably with regard to all classes of agriculture, while the granting of relief on an acreage basis, though more difficult to administer, would work out in a more equitable way. I have no criticism to offer of the way in which the five cent bonus was administered; I do not object because the landlords were not able to get the advantage of that bonus. Indeed I think that was a very wise provision. The suggestion was made from this side of the house last year that care should be taken to see that none of that money went into the hands of the mortgage companies or banks; I think the bon. member for South Battleford (Mr. ValLanee) particularly emphasized that point. It may be true-and in fact I know there were individual cases-that certain landlords should have received a part of the bonus, but to have carried out that plan would have meant the investigation of every individual lease, which in the very nature of things was impossible. So I freely admit that nothing else could have been done in that respect than was done.
That is all I desire to say at the moment, Mr. Speaker. At some future time I will avail myself of the opportunity to discuss in a more general way the conditions of agriculture and the means of affording relief.
