Mr. Speaker, until a moment ago I had not intended to say anything with respect to the resolution now before the house, but the concluding remarks of the two previous speakers seem to have indicated the attitude of the house with respect to this question. After all, the giving of this bonus is a matter of business administration, and if the house is to adopt a different method of giving assistance 'to the farmers of the west, that method must be based upon some scheme which can be administered by the government.
At the outset I must say that I am quite in accord with much that has been said by the -hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I am quite free to admit that the five cent bonus is not perfect. The government did not expect that it would be a perfect measure of relief to the farmers of western Canada. When the bonus was put through it was felt that it would meet, as well as any other method which had been suggested, the need it was intended to meet.
I agree with the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Luchkovioh), who said that the discussion this afternoon had taken in matters far beyond the scope of the resolution. But he went on to say that the resolution before

Farm Relie!-Mr. Bowman
the house was specific in character, and with that statement I entirely disagree. I cannot imagine a more vague or indefinite resolution being submitted to any legislative body. There is absolutely no suggestion in the resolution as to how this particular bonus is to be substituted for t)he five cent bonus. The hon. member for Macdonald closed his remarks by suggesting that the Minister of Agriculture should see that something was done. The hon. member for Lisgar, in concluding his remarks, stated that such help should be given as would ensure that the land which should be seeded to grain next year would be seeded, and throughout the different speeches that have been made on this subject we find this vagueness which I should think would make the resolution unacceptable to the government of 'the day.
After all, if the government is to pay out a large sum of money it must be done on some definite and distinct basis. In the resolution there is no suggestion that the new bonus, subvention or measure of relief, whatever you call it, should be based on the wheat crop. It is left very indefinite; the bonus is to be given to those farmers suffering from failure or near failure of crop. I am quite in accord with what the hon. member for Lisgar said this afternoon, that it cost those who harvested their crop more than it would if they had never cut it but simply left it in the field.
How, I would ask, is the government to estimate the difference between failure and near failure? Again, if the government is to change its plan and adopt another method of bonusing, what particular sort of failure is to be taken into consideration? Is it intended to cover the farmer who has sown his land to wheat only, or is it to cover the farmer who has sown his land to oats and barley? In the province of Manitoba the barley crop is most important. For the past year it has not been a successful crop, and the farmers have suffered a great loss. Is this resolution intended to apply to such a farmer? I submit that if the resolution is passed, it will apply to him. More than that, it opens up this whole tremendous problem, so that the farmer, no matter what branch of the industry he may be in, will be coming along asking for relief.
Why not?

That is quite proper,
but mind you we are dealing with the 1931 crop. Take an individual farmer who has had a partial crop failure:	How are you
going to indicate what the percentage of his
failure is? Or what portion of the dollar an acre or any other scheme which may be decided upon is that farmer to get? How are you going to figure it out at this late date? It seems to me that if the government adopted a scheme such as is here suggested it would cost millions of dollars to put it into operation, to get the necessary information, and to make payment on the basis of any scheme suggested by the resolution.
So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, I have nothing to say but this, that whatever relief may be given to the southern part of that province I am sure the rest of the dominion will be only too glad to pay its share. To any other part of western Canada which may have suffered from drought or hail large sums of money will have to be paid in direct relief. Large sums will have to be paid to provide seed, and it does seem to me that while the five cent bonus has not reached those farmers, nevertheless the direct relief which it will be necessary to pay will compensate, and in a great many cases more than compensate, for the five cents a bushel.
I believe it was the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young), who said, speaking of that area, that all the farmers in the district were on relief, and the figure he gave was 50,000 farmers. I understand it has been estimated that some six or seven million dollars will be required to provide seed. Perhaps I omitted, in the proper sequence of my remarks, to refer to the statement made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) that only land in fit shape for putting in crop should be considered. If we take that statement, how is the government at this date to decide, with respect to 1931, just what land in fit shape for crop is to be taken into consideration? I am sure that all hon. members on either side of the house representing rural western constituencies would be only too glad to get together and if possible devise some different bonus which would perhaps be made acceptable than the five cent bonus. Personally I should be glad to support anything of the kind, but up to the present time no better method has been suggested. The five cent bonus policy has been acted upon and at this late date I do not see that the government could adopt an entirely different policy, and one upon which no two members of the house seem to be agreed. The adoption of this resolution by the house would do nothing more than throw the matter open again; that is the only effect it would have.
There is absolutely nothing definite in the resolution. No definite proposition was suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia

Farm Relief-Mr. Hepburn
(Mr. McKenzie) when he made his speech. He filed a resolution which had been passed by one of the farmer parties in Saskatchewan, and in view of the fact that this immense problem would be thrown open once more, it seems to me an absolute impossibility for the government to adopt the scheme proposed if in fact one is suggested. For that reason and that reason only I cannot see my way clear to support the resolution, much as I should like to support any resolution which would deal more equitably with this question or with the problem of the western farmer.
Is it the hon. gentleman's interpretation of the resolution that it refers only to the 1931 crop?
Yes.
I took it that it applied to the future.

No. I was not clear on that point myself and I sent a note across to the hon. member for Assinilboia (Mr. McKenzie) who replied that it referred to the 1931 crop. Consequently my argument is along that line.

As one opposed to 'the application of a bonus of any kind so far as it applies to basic production, I want to say a word or two before voting on this resolution. To-day we are suffering from world wide overproduction due to the application of just such policies as the one here proposed. As a matter of fact, I should like to vote for the abolition of the five cent bonus entirely. We are suffering from overproduction because of acts like this one which we are asked to pass upon. Some people will say we have underconsumption, but we have overproduction so far as the basic producer is concerned so long as he is not getting cost of production. Take any basic commodity and trace the history of its marketing for the last few years and you will find that the low price is attributable to interference by meddling politicians with the law of supply and demand.
Some time ago I spoke with regard to the abrogation of the New Zealand trade treaty and I referred to what was happening in connection with the sugar industry. There,
I pointed out, was an industry which had the advantage of every possible protective tariff and bonus; but to-day the price of sugar is about 1| cents per pound so far as the basic producer is concerned, and that is due to the application of an unsound economic policy. What is wrong with wheat to-day? What is the reason for this low commodity price? 
It is due-and I say this in all kindness- to the action of some of our western friends with respect to the western wheat pool. That pool was formed primarily for the purpose of maintaining an orderly system of marketing, but instead of that the whole pool went off on a tangent and endeavoured to take out more than it put in. It disregarded the law of supply and demand and bolstered up a false price for wheat. The price was maintained as long as the pool held the wheat off the market; but unfortunately for the pool, simultaneously across the line a similar effort was made to disregard the law of supply and demand, although by a different method. President Hoover, who made promises similar to those made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) during his campaign, promised the wheat farmer a higher price for his commodity, and in an endeavour to fulfil his promise he permitted a large quantity of wheat to be kept off the market. The upshot was that between Canada and the United States we held something like four or five hundred million bushels of wheat which should have been put on the market in an orderly way, with the natural result that there was a world increase in the price of wheat. But the price was maintained only so long as we adhered to an uneconomic policy of holding marketable wheat off the open market. Other countries took advantage of the high price created by our action and sold their wheat. We held back and finally had to dump our wheat on the market, and this simply brought about chaos. It was our own fault entirely. With this condition of overproduction, does any reasonable man think that the solution is to bonus production and further aggravate the situation?
My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Porteous) mentioned the dairy farmer. In my district the dairy farmer gets 16 cents a pound for his butter, which is below cost of production. He is therefore as much entitled to a bonus out of the public treasury as the western wheat farmer, but I do not advocate any such unsound economic policy. If we have an overproduction in dairy produce, and obviously we have, the cure is not to stimulate production and thus probably aggravate the situation.
Let us look at the situation from another angle. Governments only have one source of revenue, they must tax from the pockets of the people. Admittedly we have an overproduction, but that condition is world wide and the struggle for markets is becoming fiercer. The countries which will be put out of competition in this process of elimination-we

Farm Relief-Mr. Swanston
must have a process of elimination to get back on sound economic ground-will be the countries with the highest cost of production. When we dip into the treasury to the extent of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000 and distribute that amount in an effort falsely to bolster up the production of a commodity with which the markets of the world are now glutted, we are doing an injury to the country as a whole and to the wheat producer in particular.
I do not know just how I can vote on this measure. I am sorry it emanates from this side of the house because I had hoped that we would get back once again to good, sound economic grounds. The meddling politicians who have interfered with the law of supply and demand have created this condition of chaos. I believe the only thing left for me to do is to vote against my hon. friend's motion, and, should the opportunity present itself, I intend to vote against the principle of granting a bonus to any basic commodity.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to express a word of appreciation of the extension of the bonus on wheat to the Peace river block in British Columbia. I assure the house that the people in that district appreciate the payments which have been made to them. The crop there has been quite abundant, but because of the distance from export markets a substantial amount of the value must be paid in transportation charges, and the five cent bonus has been of considerable help. The people there have asked me to express to the government their appreciation of this bonus.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution under discussion reads in part as follows:
Therefore be it resolved: that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to a more equitable and less discriminatory solution of this problem.
The resolution does not suggest any new method of meeting the difficulty. Certain portions of the constituency of Maple Creek were able to produce small amounts of wheat, and naturally those farmers who were able to grow some wheat are very appreciative of the bonus. However, along with others, I was unfortunate enough not to be able to produce any wheat; therefore I received no benefit from the bonus. At the time the budget was brought down on June 1 we had no idea that there would be a crop failure. Later on in the session, when we found that a crop failure would occur, the western Conservative members interviewed the government to see if the bonus could be put on an
acreage basis. We were told that there were difficulties which could not be surmounted and that it would have to continue as a five cent per bushel bonus.
With reference to the suggestion that a dollar per acre be paid, I know that the people in the territories which were dried out and where there was no crop will be quite * willing to accept anything. If, after carrying the burden of relief and supplying seed for this year, the government can see its way clear to give us one dollar or more per acre, I am sure it will be greatly appreciated.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, in continuing for
a brief time the debate on the resolution moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) I intend to refer to the remarks of a number of the previous speakers.

If this legislation is inequitable, if it is unfair and unjust, the government should come to the rescue and make it fair and just. There should

Oh, oh!

Do you produce any
mules?

That movement on the part of the Conservative party in Canada practically ruined or wiped out live stock raising in that part of Saskatchewan which I represent in the House of Commons. The Liberal party would broaden it out in order to build on it sound legislation. Fear is always dissociated from any policy of the Liberal party. It is a tradition of the Liberal party to deal with a problem courageously and go through with it to the end. Consequently the policy I am advocating is not a policy of fear, neither is it a policy to be applied to one branch of agriculture and not to another branch. The Conservative party are ready to apply the bonus or bounty principle to one branch of our industrial life, but they are afraid to apply it to the other. That to my mind is not sound policy; it is an unstable foundation upon which to build a great dominion. Since, this policy is applicable only to wheat growing and not to the other divisions of agriculture, perhaps, as I said before, it grows out of the national policy of my hon. friends opposite, and as such it is false and should not be supported.
Sure.

As my hon. friend opposite says, "sure," obviously he shares my view that we cannot build up Canada into a great manufacturing and agricultural country by' trying to bind all parts of the dominion together by bonuses and other similar means.

portions; in a word, our approach should be scientific. If we were to pursue the policy of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), a policy formulated outside of ou-r universities or parliament, we would ignore all intellectuality and not get very far.

-help, aid, succour, support.
Murray's New English Dictionary gives this definition:
The action of helping or aiding in an undertaking or necessity; furtherance, succour, the help afforded, aid, support, relief.
Now, let us take the dictionary meaning of relief:
Relief: payment varying in value or kind, aid, help, assistance in money towards saving something.
In other words the term "assistance" means "relief;" and the term "relief" means "assistance." Now, things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another; therefore the term assistance simply means relief; and the term relief simply means assistance. That is all there is to it. So there is no use wasting any more time about that.
I want to prove in another way that the term assistance means relief, and I propose to do so out of the mouth of the Prime Minister himself. When he introduced this measure on July 24, 1931, he advanced three arguments in support of it. The first argument was the low price of wheat; the next, this low price of wheat in relation to the cost of production up to that time; and the last argument was expressed in these words:
The third reason is the necessity of a measure of relief for western Canadian producers.
According to the statement made by the Prime Minister on the floor of this House of Commons, this bonus legislation was at best a relief measure. I want to make that plain in order that the people of western Canada may be put right in connection with it.
Now before concluding, let me say that we may divide the resolution into three parts. The first statement is that the legislation of last year was unjust and unfair. I do not think there is any doubt about that. The next point is that it was so unjust and so unfair that the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities took up that unfairness and unjustness and, as a result, petitioned the government. That association covers Saskatchewan from one end to the other; it
represents the rural municipal life of the whole province, and consequently it means something. In that connection we say that since the legislation was unjust, unfair and inequitable, and since it did not appeal to the province of Saskatchewan or to western Canada the cabinet should come forward courageously and reshape this legislation into something that will have more appeal to the farmers of the prairie provinces.
In that connection may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am only too glad to commend the Prime Minister and his cabinet for going as far as they have gone in this direction. I do not think it is sound, but there may be the argument of emergency in its favour. I know from where it comes; I know what is back of it, but in the present emergency in western Canada I would be the last to say that the farmers in my riding who received the five cents per bushel should not be thankful for it. But throughout my riding I made it plain that although many of the farmers in the constituency of North Battleford received five cents a bushel for the wheat they produced, in accepting that bonus they should be very careful not to allow the government or the Conservative party of Canada at the same time to sell them the principle of protection, because after all is said and done a five cent sop is not enough to sell agriculture in this country into protective bondage for all time.
Might I say further, Mr. Speaker, that in the riding of North Battleford the average wheat production would be perhaps 30 bushels to the acre which, at 5 cents a bushel, would mean $1.50 per acre. Therefore, as far as the constituency of North Battleford is concerned, I do not see that any great benefit will come from this proposed legislation. There are some parts of the riding down towards Saskatoon where the average production would be only from eight to ten bushels to the acre, and in those districts a limited number of farmers might receive 50 cents, 40 cents, or 25 cents more per acre. That would be helpful. Beyond that they would not benefit by this legislation at all. I am speaking for the rest of the province and for the farmers throughout western Canada. If the SI per seeded acre bonus could be applied generally all over the west, the money paid in the areas where relief has been necessary could be applied on the amount spent for all such relief.
While I am on this point let me say that I think this note business is wrong. I do not know who initiated it, whether it was planned by the Prime Minister or by his cabinet, but
Farm Relief-Mr. McIntosh

some person is responsible for it. They tell us legislation is initiated in the House of Commons, by the cabinet and sometimes in the office of the Prime Minister. Well, some person initiated this giving of a note in each case of relief, and what I fear in connection with it is that each of these notes may be held as a political club at election time. If that is the case that is enough for me; I would go out and fight my own party on a principle of that kind. Why take the note at all? There are thousands of merchants in Canada carrying accounts ranging from S100 to SI,000 without notes. They have trusted their customers and they are likely to get more money in that way than the government may ever receive through these notes. So I say these notes should be discontinued, and a policy adopted which will be more just to the farmers of western Canada.
In closing may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I support this resolution. I do not think it is sound from the point of view of my constituency, my province or this dominion, but I am supporting it because for the time being we cannot get rid of the national policy out of which it has grown. Therefore, in order to help the farmers in an emergency I am only too willing to stand in my place in parliament and say that if the government in its wisdom could go further and grant a bonus of SI for every acre seeded, I believe in the long run we would be further ahead. I say this although I am opposed to the principle of the resolution, because I believe public money would not be wasted, as much of it is now, by so doing.
Let me make one further observation. Had the Liberal principle of unemployment insurance been adopted fifteen or twenty years ago in this country we could have had built up by now a sum of money sufficient to take care of our industrial workers for several years. We could have had millions of dollars in a fund of that kind, which would be available for individual unemployment relief purposes. The money we are spending to-day, in many ways uselessly, in trying to help the industrially unemployed, could be used in behalf of agriculture, for the benefit of those who have had no crops, those who are destitute and others who could be put on a better basis by spending national funds in a legitimate way to help them through a trying emergency until they would be able to care for themselves.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by endorsing the resolution and hoping the house may take favourable action upon it.

We have had a fairly wide discussion of the motion itself, as well as of almost every other subject which, directly or indirectly, could be related to the motion. As I understand it, this resolution has brought about a discussion on the granting of a bonus on the wheat raised in western Canada as opposed to the granting of a bonus, on an acreage basis, to those who may undertake to raise wheat. The question which naturally suggests itself is whether it is a wiser plan to extend the bonus to those who have produced wheat in western Canada or, on the other hand, to extend it to those who prepare acreage, actually producing or not producing wheat as the case may be.
The principle of the bonus, judging from the attitude of the mover of the resolution, is not condemned; it seems to be accepted as a good thing. When we come to the purpose of the government in regard to this matter, I take it that they propose to advance to the producers of wheat certain assistance, and they have some reasons for so doing. Turning to Hansard of 1931 I find at page 2171 the following announcements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett):
The third matter to which attention might be directed is that touching the movement of wheat. There has been a succession of bad harvests in some parts of western Canada, and during the last few weeks lack of moisture-I speak subject to correction, I hope- has caused a loss of this year's prospective crop in a great deal of that area. My advices by telephone were that very few days would determine the fate of a considerable portion of the crop. In some parts of the country this is the third crop failure and the reserves of the people are entirely exhausted. Two things must happen: First, provision should be made to assist those who have a crop, because they have considerable obligations, taxes, etc., which must be discharged. Other methods will be taken to deal with the situation of the provinces which are not in a position to assist those who with their reserves exhausted and their crops a failure for the third time are practically ruined.
I think the statement there .sets out fairly that relief is to be given and the purpose of the government with respect to the matter.
Why did the government extend assistance to the wheat growers in western Canada, particularly to the prairie provinces? That I think is also explained in the statement made by the Prime Minister. Let us go back and consider the circumstances that obtained for many years leading up to the crop of last year. We know that the farmers of western Canada, as in no other part of the dominion, were encouraged to concentrate to a very considerable degree on the growing of wheat. They were so encour-

Farm Relief-Mr. Stanley
aged not only by governmental agencies and by their own organizations but also by transportation, financial and banking institutions, as well as by other organizations in the country. They all encouraged the farmer to concentrate on the growing of wheat in western Canada.
Now, coming to the situation that existed at the time this statement was made, the house will recall that wheat had gone down very rapidly. There was a crash and it meant that economic conditions in western Canada would be very serious indeed. As a result the government undertook to give a bonus upon the wheat which was to be produced. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) in the course of his speech made the statement that in a large measure the crash in the price of wheat was due to the attitude taken by the wheat pool of western Canada. That statement of course is not substantiated by the facts; indeed, it is ridiculous to those of us in western Canada who know something about the proceedings of the wheat pool. While I am not here to defend the actions of the wheat pool-they can take care of themselves -I must point out that they had very little to do with any change in the price of wheat or with the determination of the world price of grain on the British market. The fact is that we found ourselves in such a position that we simply had to take for our grain on the British market precisely what the rest of the world was taking. The amount of wheat held by the wheat pool in Canada, even granting that they purposely held as large a quantity as some people say that they held, did not have a great deal to do with the crash that came in the price of this commodity. We all know now what has happened during the many months that have succeeded. The world wide financial crash and the financial conditions which have obtained ever since were to a very considerable extent the factor which brought down the price of wheat and which has kept it down to the very low level it has since maintained. This I say in justification of the salesmanship of the organizations in western Canada and not in justification of the local attitude taken by the grain organization out in those provinces.
Coming to the justification of the bonus, 1 am not going to take up very much time discussing the principle of it. The fact is that we have long since passed the point in this country-and the same is true of any other civilized country in the world to-day- where we are left with much choice as to what we are going to do in regard to duties, subventions, bonuses and so forth. Free trade countries no longer exist. The restrictions of 41761-22
trade, if you want to put it that way, that are found necessary in the various countries of the world, exist largely as a matter of self defence, and we are in exactly the same position in western Canada. I can say, speaking as one who comes from the west and who has had very much to do with the farmers of western Canada, that it does not hurt my conscience one bit, and I am quite satisfied that it does not hurt the conscience of many a western farmer, to take the bonus which is given through this five cents a bushel on wheat. When, in common with all other countries, we are extending duties, subventions, bonuses and so forth, we are simply giving a portion of one of these forms of assistance to the farmers of the west by way of a five cent bonus on wheat. One justification for the five cent bonus has been given, and another justification for it has been intimated in the statement of the Prime Minister. Taxes have to be paid, business has to be carried on as usual, and municipal and provincial obligations have to be met. Who are going to meet them? Well, to a large extent out in our province they are going to be met by the farmers who have to pay their taxes. The farmer who produced the grain and who suffered from this drop in price will be the one who will meet this obligation, not the farmer who has had no crop for the past three seasons. If the province is to carry on, if the school districts are to be kept intact, if different municipal undertakings are to be carried out, these are the people who must meet the obligation. The help granted to them by the bonus of five cents per bushel has not made them plutocrats, although it has helped them out a little.
The suggestion has been made that the bonus should be paid on an acreage basis. In my opinion that would be impracticable. This government has no organization in the west whereby it could determine the number of acres upon which payment should be made. It would require an army of inspectors to offset the many attempts which would be made at deception. The administration of such legislation would be impossible with the present organization.
The -payment of a bonus on a bushel basis is an altogether different proposition. As the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turn-bull) has pointed out, the bonus is one thing, but there is also the granting of relief in the broadest sense of the word. If relief is to be given by the different- governments and municipalities, it would have to be upon an entirely different basis. It must be granted -to those who need it, and that could not be done on

Farm, Relief-Mr. Blair

an acreage basis. To do that would not be to extend relief in the real acceptation of the term. It would be granting a bonus only to those engaged in the grain business, but there are others who should receive assistance according to their actual needs.
I agree with the argument made by hon. members on both sides of the house as to the need of relief in various parts of the western provinces. The southern part of Saskatchewan and certain parts of Alberta require relief on a rather extensive scale, but it should be granted without any relation to a bonus on the production of wheat.
The next question is as to how this. relief should be granted, and here the matter of jurisdiction of the various governments comes in. As I understand it, it would be impossible for the federal government to undertake a relief program in a municipality in Alberta without consulting both the provincial and the municipal authorities. To grant relief on an acreage basis would necessitate a complete understanding as to the respective jurisdictions of the federal, provincial and municipal authorities.
The hon. members in the United Farmers of Alberta section of the house appear to me to be in one breath praising the government for having spent approximately $5,000,000, and in the next saying exactly the opposite. This they have done not only in this house but in the convention recently held. There seems to be a certain degree of duplicity in their actions, and one cannot help but think that when they utter their commendation they do so with their tongues in their cheeks. This is borne out by the fact that they were ready to pass a resolution which commends the government for what it has done, and then goes on to demand something else. I have no objection to the United Farmers of Alberta or any other organization demanding an extension of this bonus, but I want it distinctly understood that when the suggestion goes abroad that the farmers of Alberta are not grateful to the government which gave that assistance from the public treasury, those who make the suggestion are expressing a sentiment which does not exist among the rank and file of the farmers of that province. Nor do I feel that, farmer representatives or even the United Farmers in their convention have the right to speak for the great bulk of the fanners of that province, particularly when they approach the subject with the attitude which has been manifested in their discussion of this question, notably in their discussion of it on the floor of their convention.

Just as was said yesterday by another hon. member in the discussion of this matter, I want the eastern representatives in this house to feel that the people of the west, and certainly the farmers of our province, are thankful for the assistance they have received. When we require more assistance by way of seed grain and of aid to those who are destitute, having regard to the financial condition of the government of our province, in all probability we shall have to come back to this government and parliament to ask for further assistance for the men and their families who are suffering. Without entering into the party politics of our province, I am sorry to say that what has occurred in our provincial legislature during the last two years makes it evident that we shall certainly have to look to the federal government to provide us with the funds to carry on the. necessary work of our province. This being so, I want to be able to feel as a representative from that province that when we approach this parliament and this administration, they will realize that we are grateful for the assistance they are giving.
In conclusion, very often I think an entirely wrong interpretation of the conditions prevailing is given to the house and to the eastern part of Canada by our representatives from the west. The position of our farmers and of the residents of our cities, towns and villages is not as desperate as it is represented to be. That spirit of optimism, of determination, of courageousness that enabled them in years gone by to overcome the obstacles which presented themselves on every hand, still exists, and they are still going ahead. While we shall have to assist many farmers as well as many residents of our towns and cities, and continue to assist them for a time, there is that spirit of determination to make good which has always prevailed in the west. I bring it as a final word in this discussion, that while at times we may appear to criticize unduly, we still have left a spirit of thankfulness and optimism, and the courage to make good.

Mr. Speaker, I could not let this opportunity pass without registering my disapproval of the motion which is before the house. I cannot understand how the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) could maintain that the farmers' organizations can approve of this. It seems to me it is against the principle of all farmers' organizations or any Liberal organization and is opposed to the principle of many Conservatives, that is the idea of subsidizing or bonusing anything that is not standing on

Farm Relief-Mr. Boyes
its own feet. So long as it is a matter of charity, we cannot disapprove of it when it is necessary, but to uphold some industry that cannot stand on its own feet is quite a different problem and has to be considered very seriously.
The farmers of Ontario have assisted and nobly assisted the western provinces. In the first place they assisted them to develop their natural resources, and when the time came, those natural resources were handed over to the western provinces to be controlled by them. If the western provinces have difficulties, then those difficulties should be looked after largely by the west, except in the case of extreme necessity when they cannot cope with the situation and then the federal government should be asked to assist. But we must realize that many Ontario farmers are also growing wheat and many of them have crop failures. A winter like the present one almost ensures a crop failure for the coming season. No one is subsidizing the Ontario farmers. I do not see why the farmers of Ontario, having assisted the people of the west in their early years, having given them all the natural resources which belonged to them, should be expected to subsidize those who are their competitors. The farmer of the west can grow grain much more easily than the Ontario farmer can; he can raise sheep much cheaper than the Ontario farmer can, and I do not see why the Ontario farmer should be asked to subsidize the farmer of the west. As a matter of charity it might be all right, but I object to the principle of subsidizing when the necessity for charity does not exist.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few observations in connection with the resolution before the house. Last year when this matter was under discussion I heartily concurred in the action which was taken by the government. At that time I fully realized that the producers of wheat in the west had their difficulties. The price was low and surely some assistance was required. We from the most westerly part of eastern Canada felt it our duty, when any other portion of the dominion was in distress, to render assistance in order that the situation might be relieved. I heartily concurred in the granting of five cents a bushel on the wheat for the prairie provinces. I am more than surprised to-day to hear a number of hon. members opposite expressing themselves as they are. They are 41761-22J
disagreeing with the principle that was adapted last year; they are saying that they wish it carried out in a different manner this year, and in fact a number of them have gone almost so far as to say that they disapprove of the five cent bonus. I am very gflad to know that the speakers on this side of the house who come from the west express a different view. They know that the farmers of the west who are raising wheat have certainly been very thankful for the bonus of five cents a bushel.
I should like to express the view of one who comes from the western part of the province of Ontario, from the riding of East Middlesex. In western Ontario we do produce some wheat, but we also raise a great many other farm products. We are engaged to a great extent in the dairying business. W e manufacture butter and produce milk for many purposes, the chief of which is the manufacture of cheese. We have not heard very much in this house regarding the manufacture of cheese, which is carried on to quite an extent in western Ontario, and more so in eastern Ontario, very nice revenue having until recently been received from this source. Last year when this five cents a bushel bonus was granted, the price of wheat was low, but to-day it is considerably higher. On the other hand, cheese was higher in price a year ago than it is to-day, and the same applies to other dairy products. As I say, we granted the bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat because wheat was low in price at that time and we wished to relieve the distress in the west. It is quite true that we did that and did it cheerfully. But for the coming year things do look somewhat different from last year. As I said before, I am very willing to help the west. We did so last year. We carried out the program which we had in mind. But so far as the coming year is concerned, a demand is arising from certain parts of the province of Ontario that other agricultural products besides wheat be bonused. My own view is this, that in view of the financial condition of the country to-day it is possibly a little away from the mark to expect that we may continue to do as was done last year, and hon. gentlemen opposite who are trying to increase the bonus by putting it on an acreage basis are possibly defeating their own ends by not favouring the scheme which the government put into effect last year. So far as I am concerned I feel that for the coming year, in order to give

Farm Relief-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
satisfaction to our farmers in the east who are having their own troubles-the pri-ce of their cheese is depressed due to the fact that to a great extent it is exported to England where the depression is being felt, resulting in a lower price than we got before, for cheese-as well as for other dairy products-we should discontinue the bonus on wheat.

I think the majority of the hon.
members who have spoken have found themselves more or less at a loss due to the unfortunate circumstances that this resolution was not much more definitely worded. Had it been worded as definitely as it exists in the mind of the hon. member who moved the resolution* it would naturally have fallen into three parts. First, what was the intention of this five cent bonus? What elements went to make up the five cents? If it were granted as a solution of some particular problem, and if later another different problem arose, should the same remedy be applied, or should there be another solution of the new problem? Next, would it be compatible with the financial obligations resting upon the government to do what has been suggested by many of the speakers? I had not intended to take . up more than five minutes in what I have to say on this resolution, but I think hon. members will agree that I am forced into the position of deviating to a certain extent from the resolution itself to reply to some of the statements that have been made. I shall however be as brief as possible, having regard to what I have suggested.
First, what led to this bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat? Speaking for myself, before entering this so-called realm of politics I found that many farmers in western Canada had followed very closely the policies of the different political parties in Canada and had come to the conclusion that in one respect the two major parties seemed to be at one, namely that they were both protectionist. Whether or not it was due to a more astute political leadership, I think the average person in the west will agree that there was created in western Canada a feeling on the part of a certain section of the public that the Conservatives were protectionist and that the Liberals were against protection, although, as I have stated, the majority of the people felt that both parties were protectionist. The result of this public opinion which had been created, whether wittingly or not for the purpose, was that there arose in the west a certain division of feeling, a certain resentment,

against the so-called financial interests and the manufacturers, including the implement manufacturers, in the east. That was the regrettable thing in connection with this policy, presented as it was. When therefore I accepted the office I have been called upon to occupy I felt that whatever in my humble way I could do to break down that division that had been set up would be some slight contribution to this country of which we are all so proud. Accordingly I took the first available opportunity at the short session of discussing the problem with members on this side of the house, and particularly with some of the members of the United Farmers group from Alberta and Saskatchewan. They agreed with me that if it was possible, in addition to protection, to make some arrangement by which this division could be overcome, something would be accomplished.
There were many varying elements and circumstances to take into consideration. I think we all agree that the one class of agriculturist that receives less protection from the tariff than any other is the wheat farmer of the west, chiefly because the great preponderance of his production is forced into export. Therefore I set out to find in the most generous way I eould what these straight wheat farmers did pay on account of the tariff for their machinery and equipment more than they would have had to pay had there been no tariff. I was very much surprised at the estimate I arrived at, because I must admit that I myself felt that the effects of the tariff were much more considerable than the conclusion to which I was forced to come.
I went with this proposition to my chief, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). It appealed to him. The problem was: how to provide some compensating adjustment for this particular class of people. The matter was brought before the cabinet, and in the discussion that arose as to what could be done of a compensating nature, it was found to be so small per bushel that finally another item came up that is very near to those of us who are western farmers, and produce wheat-the price of wheat had sunk so low that the proportion of the freight to its price was much greater than it had been when prices were what we had been pleased to consider more normal. It was finally agreed that some assistance should be given in the nature of a bonus to help decrease the disadvantages proportionately to the price of wheat at that time. I think that this is as direct and clear a statement as I can give with reference to the five cent bonus. It was, as I have stated, for the

Farm Relief-Mr. Weir (Melfort)
solution, to a certain extent, of more than one particular problem in western Canada.
At the conclusion of the session we found in western Canada a problem of a different nature-the greatest problem that has arisen in this country so far as agriculture is concerned-the calamity arising from the drought condition in the prairie provinces, particularly in Saskatchewan. It was decided that I should go to Saskatchewan on account of the nature of this difficulty, and devote a great part of my time in cooperation with the provincial government and with the farmers of that province to seeing what could be done for the alleviation of this calamity. I did so, with the result that since last session I have spent practically seven weeks in Saskatchewan with the exception of some short time in Alberta and Manitoba. The nature of the work was such, and the demand on one's time so great, that although I own a farm in the province I have been able to spend only two days on it since the election in 1930. So my time was devoted to this work, and to this work solely during those seven weeks.
What condition did I find in western Canada? I realize that it has not a direct bearing on the resolution, yet it has been referred to in so many different ways during this debate that I feel it is only fair to the house that having made a personal survey I should give in the simplest form some idea of what I found. There was an area of seventy-six municipalities that had practically no crop of any kind for three years. Hon. members in this house who have not been west and who have read certain misrepresentations in the eastern press, due to lack of correct information, and those who have heard from other sources various presentations of the case, will, I am sure, be surprised to realize -at least those who have thought that a great deal of that area should not have been devoted to farming-that most of the land in those seventy-six municipalities has produced more agricultural wealth per capita than perhaps any other area in this dominion. The farmers there never knew anything in the nature of a crop failure. Year after year until three years ago in the Regina plains between Regina and Moose Jaw and in the area south the land yielded 25, 30 and 35 bushels per acre of the best wheat produced in the west. Their farm homes were unexcelled anywhere. Not only that, but their live stock was of a very high quality. Many people have the idea that in that part of the country there are nothing but cayuses and scrub live stoek, and on many farms no live stock at all. The best indication that I can give hon. members
of the quality of that live stock is that the greatest percentage of the live stock from Saskatchewan that came year after year to compete with the best live stock from the different parts of this country and from the republic to the south carried off much more than their share of honours on the basis of numbers. The wheat production in that area alone for the fifteen years before the first crop failure averaged over 83,000,000 bushels. That will help the house, I hope, to realize the problem that we had to deal with. It was not a question of moving the people away after the successive good crops that they had had for so many years, but of holding them there and assisting them financially and otherwise as far as was in our power, until a cessation of the present difficulties. There was another area consisting of ninety-six municipalities in which there had been two practically complete crop failures; a third area of sixty-four municipalities in which there was a crop failure last year for the first time in the past three years. Practically two-thirds, if not more, of the cultivated land in this great province of Saskatchewan had been dealt this unprecedented staggering blow, and this was the problem we had to face.
Some of you, perhaps, within sound of my voice have been inclined to ask: If the farmers there have produced that great amount of wealth within ten years, then why was it not possible for them to withstand the difficulties in which they have found themselves? Let me say that the extent of the area is something like old eastern Ontario from Toronto to the Quebec border, but larger in extent, where for years we have had some of the thriftiest and most scientific farmers in the country. They have practised diversified, balanced farming with a skill perhaps unexcelled by any other people in this country. Yet how many of those farmers, if for three years in succession they did not have anything in the nature of a crop, not even sufficient to feed their live stock, and were therefore forced to dispose of it, except so much as would provide the very necessities of life, and with respect to which the government have to assist them-how many, I say, of those farmers could stand a blow like that without some help? The only way in which they could have done it was perhaps to have hoarded their wealth somewhere. But the average man, I think, in the east as well as in the west, after making a reasonable allowance for the future invested his money in stocks and other investments that even to the best financiers seemed absolutely sound but proved far otherwise.

We felt that if ever there was a time when the question should be handled in a manner absolutely free from prejudice, this question should be handled in that way. Therefore it was decided that it should be handled absolutely free from political interference of any kind, and a relief commission was appointed. We selected five commissioners, with Henry Black as chairman, after interviewing some of the most successful business and professional men in Regina and Moose Jhw. We discussed the problem for a few moments and pictured those people who have had no money for three years, with practically no clothing and no reserve strength. with a clear title, with no encumbrance in the way of mortgages, we who have contributed so much to the country are not going to be reduced to the condition of receiving charity. That was their position and they insisted that

they be given the privilege of repaying. That was the first time that question came up. The question before us is this: What are we to do with people who have been hit as they have been hit in Saskatchewan? What are we to do that will be just to them in view of the whole picture as we have it? Outside of the seventy-six municipality area our obligations are in conjunction with those of the provincial government; and in the drought area in Alberta and Manitoba, as in Saskatchewan, the percentage that we bear, if we bear any percentage of the loss, has yet to be determined. I explained the whole proposition to these men and they seemed to be satisfied. They realized the problem we were facing; they knew that we had to make certain that every man, woman and child in that area should be clothed warmly enough to meet the winter, that fuel should 'be provided before the first blizzard came along, that potatoes should be in the cellars before the winter came on, as it does sometimes with very little warning. They realized that large sums of money would be required to provide feed for their stock, and that on top of that additional sums would be required-amounting to $5,000,000 in Saskatchewan alone-to seed the land this spring. Even though a census be taken with the greatest care I think that those of us who are farmers will agree that it would not be very accurate. It 'has been the rage of late in western Canada 'to try to obtain all kinds of statistics, and I know in connection with my own farm that information 'has been given when I was absent which was not at all accurate. The best example of this is the attempt to collect information in connection with our program of restricted areas. I have an amendment to propose to the house in connection with the second reading of this bill.
I think it is well known to members of the house that throughout this capital city, and in fact throughout Canada, sinister reflections have been circulated concerning members of the Civil Service Commission which tend, if they are not answered, to discredit the competency, efficiency and reliability of that commission. The matter of appointments to the civil service, especially appointments to what is known as the outside service, also on several occasions has been under discussion in this chamber, but in such discussions neither mem-
bers of the Civil Service Commission nor officials or employees of the civil service of Canada have been able to participate.
Therefore it has appeared advisable that members of the Civil Service Commission and representatives of the civil service of Canada should have an opportunity to be heard before this house should adopt the pending resolution moved by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) and before second reading is given Bill No. 14, which second reading has been moved this evening by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon).
It has seemed to me, as the nominal representative in this house of the Civil Service Commission, that such hearing could be best afforded by the appointment of a special committee of seven members of the house, representing all political parties in this house. It also has appeared advisable that the widest possible authority should be given such committee to inquire into and report generally upon the administration and operation of the Civil Service Act, with power to advise this house as such committee may deem advisable concerning the repeal or amendment of any of the existing provisions of the Civil Service Act, or the substitution therefor or addition thereto of other provisions which will tend to ensure the efficient administration of that act.
It is within the memory of older members of the house that a royal commission on the civil service was appointed in 1908 which made a very voluminous report. In 1919 a special committee of this house made an inquiry and report concerning the inside service. Subsequently, in 1923, a special committee of this house was appointed to inquire into and report upon the operation of the Civil Service Act, of which committee Hon. James Malcolm was chairman. This committee also made a very extensive inquiry and report. Again in 1924 a special committee of the Senate made an inquiry and report on the civil service. All these reports were printed and published, and I think are now available for the consideration of members of this house. Nevertheless, the committee which I am about to propose will necessarily undertake very onerous duties and responsibilities. Although I am to be a member of that committee, I certainly accept that duty with very great reluctance indeed.

I consider legislation which deprives a minister of the right to make an appointment and empowers a lawyer who is not even an employee of the Department of Justice to fill a position in that department, is unwise, unsound and ought to be amended.

I assure hon. members opposite that I am not approaching this question in any partisan spirit, because while some bad nominations have been made under Liberal administrations, some bad nominations have also been made under Conservative administrations. I want to approach the question in a broad spirit. It is all very well to say: We do not want to return to the patronage system. We want the nominations to be aboveboard, but while we are desirous of having the merit system, let us find a scheme which will be based on true merit and let the true merit system prevail. Let us do away with that camouflage system which has produced such bad results and has given birth to complaints all over Canada.
41761-23J
I do not want to dwell at length on this question; I think I have made my point sufficiently clear, and I ask that this bill be now read a second time.

Before the hon. member concludes his address on this particular bill, would he be good enough to explain to the house the reasons for the major change urged in 'the bill, namely, the exclusion of the outside service? That is an aspect of the bill he has not yet discussed.

I shall be pleased to
answer briefly the question put by the hon. member for Bow River. I have already stated that the three commissioners sitting at Ottawa cannot really be the best judges of the qualifications of all the different employees living outside the city. I have already pointed out that these three men cannot be an encyclopaedia of science. They are not properly qualified to ascertain the qualifications of a man who wants to be appointed caretaker of a customs house in Vancouver, or a postmaster in the Yukon or a customs officer in the port of Gaspe. Therefore I think in the best interests of the civil service itself, it is better that the three commissioners sitting in Ottawa should devote themselves to applications and nominations for positions in the inside service alone. They will find that a hard enough job, because in the inside service theTe are at least 18,000 employees. The appointment of a postmaster, for instance, in any part of Canada could be better made by the minister of the department than by the Civil Service Commission. I might point out to the hon. member for Bow River that on the twenty-fourth of June of last year the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself stated that in the legislation of 1918 they had gone too far in putting the postmasters throughout Canada under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. It is not necessary for me to speak any longer, but I think the public interest will be best served by taking the outside service out of the jurisdiction of the commission; or, if the committee which is to be formed prefers, by devising other ways and means of appointing candidates to the outside service.
How does the hon. gentleman propose to appoint such outside candidates?

I do not think that at this stage of the proceedings it would be proper for me to answer all these questions, especially
Civil Service Act

in view of the fact that there will be ample opportunity to answer them in committee. I am pleased to see that my hon. friend is a member of the committee because I am sure he will have some very good suggestions to offer.

I am astonished, but at the same time I am not surprised, that this evening we should have a proposal from the ranks of the Conservative party of a character that is calculated almost entirely to destroy the Civil Service Act which that party is responsible for putting on the statute book of this country.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Is it not a fact that the previous speaker closed the debate?
The hon. member for Bow River is quite in order in addressing the house.

It is also interesting to note that until I asked him the question after he bad sat down the first time, the mover of the motion (Mr. Gagnon) did not give any explanation whatever of the most .sinister proposal in the bill, that of turning *over to the greediest of hordes the patronage [DOT]of the various constituencies throughout this 'dominion. The Secretary of State (Mr. Caban), when he spoke a few moments ago on an amendment that was ruled out of order, proposed that this bill and the resolution standing in the name of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) should be referred to a special committee, and he gave two chief reasons for that. The first was that there were certain sinister reflections upon the present Civil Service Commission which in the public interest should be examined into and cleared up.

And concerning which they
should be heard.

Yes. He said that neither the representatives of the Civil Service Commission nor those of the rank and file of the civil service had had an opportunity to defend themselves in connection with these allegations. The other reason he gave was that we might devise ways and means of improving on the Civil Service Act and its administration.
In regard to all these proposals of the Secretary of State, I, and I believe my colleagues are in complete accord. We think it advisable that there should be an examination into the actual conditions under which the administration of the civil service is being conducted to-day by the Civil Service Commission, and I will go so far as to agree with
fMr. Gagnon.]
my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) and join hands with him in a dismissal of the present civil service commissioners. I have no hesitation in saying that, from what meagre knowledge I have of what has been going on for some years and is now beginning to come out in the public press; but to destroy the merit principle-never. This country cannot afford to do that at this stage.
It is within a few minutes of eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and as I wish to discuss the principle of this bill at some length, I ask you to call it eleven o'clock.
If the hon. member wishes to bring the debate to a close he should move to adjourn the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We can call it eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, if the house agrees.
As I was saying a moment ago when the opposition with its usual courtesy declined me the privilege of having it called eleven o'clock-
Not the opposition, the government.
No, not the opposition. Strangely enough I think I have had more courtesy at the hands of the late government than I have had at the hands of this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about. I asked the Speaker to call it eleven o'clock and he declined.
I did not hear my hon. friend. Will he please accept my sincere regrets.
I did not understand the Minister of Justice. If it is the desire of the house to call it eleven o'clock, it is eleven o'clock.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
